sections.html:
Lexington sits about 12 miles west of Columbia and serves as the Lexington County seat. It is also the most populous town in the county. Since 2000 the town has grown the way a Columbia bedroom community does, so buyers often trade off lake access, school zone and commute time.

U.S. Route 1, known locally as Augusta Highway, cuts through town, and Lake Murray lies just north. Downtown has older properties while the edges hold newer subdivisions, which means one block can look nothing like the next in age, condition and price.

The town counted 9,793 people in 2000, 17,870 in 2010 and 23,568 in 2020. Here is how the housing side looks:

Housing measureLexington town
Households, 2020 Census9,462
Housing units, 2020 Census10,211
Share of units vacant7.3%
Owner-occupied rate, 2020 to 202468.7%
Median home value, 2020 to 2024$297,700
Median gross rent, 2020 to 2024$1,545

Treat the median value as a rough backdrop. Your own house will be priced by its condition, its lot and what comparable sales nearby show. A place that needs a new roof sells for less than a move-in ready neighbor, whatever the town-wide median says.

The lake dates to 1930, and a dam about 1.7 miles long holds it back, roughly 5 miles north of town. Lake Murray is the town's best known feature and draws buyers who want to be near the water.

If your parcel sits close to the shore, expect extra questions about water access, dock permits and flood zone paperwork. Plenty of Lexington houses never deal with any of that. Your title company can tell you what applies to your lot, and it is worth asking before you name a price.

Everything permit related runs through the Town's Planning and Building Department at 111 Maiden Lane. Hours are Monday to Friday, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. Phone numbers by purpose:

  • Main line: 803-356-5938
  • Inspection scheduling: 803-358-7267
  • Code enforcement: 803-358-1589

The department also looks at proposed businesses for land use compliance when a business license is requested. If you are fixing something up before you sell, ask whether the work needs a permit. Skipped permits tend to surface when a buyer's attorney or lender starts asking questions, and that can stall a conventional closing.

Also check the boundary. A Lexington mailing address does not guarantee the parcel is inside the town limits, so confirm that with the town before you pick an office to call.

sections.h2: Property tax due dates and penalties
sections.html:
Lexington County sends the bill. State law makes taxes payable between September 30 and January 15, then stacks penalties: 3% once January 15 passes, a further 7% after February 1 and a further 5% after March 16.

A legal residence is assessed at 4%, while other real property is assessed at 6%. If you owe back taxes when you sell, the title company normally settles them from your proceeds at the closing table, so an old balance is a nuisance but rarely a dealbreaker.

Real property owners can opt into a county installment plan. It breaks the year into five advance payments, each 16.67% of the prior year's tax, due February 15, April 15, June 15, August 15 and October 15. The remaining balance comes due January 15.

You must get your application in before January 15. The plan leaves out escrowed taxes and personal vehicles, so if your lender already pays the tax bill for you, the plan is not an option.

sections.h2: Recording a deed in Lexington County
sections.html:
Deeds go to the Register of Deeds at 212 S. Lake Dr., Suite 301, which also handles mortgages, liens and plats. Searching is available online back to August 1, 1984. Electronic filing works through partners such as Simplifile and CSC.

Since March 1, 2018, taxable or exempt transfers need an affidavit. Do not put Social Security or bank account numbers on a recorded document unless the law demands them. The state deed fee runs $1.85 per $500 of value.

sections.h2: Selling with problems in the way
sections.html:
Owners who try a standard listing in Lexington commonly bump into one of these:

  • A roof or cooling system that a buyer's inspector will point at
  • Past work done without a permit, which the Town's building office may ask about
  • An estate or probate delay after an owner has died
  • Back taxes and penalties from a missed January 15 deadline

Heat is the main wear factor on local roofs and air conditioning, so a unit that has run through many summers is worth having looked at before the first showing. In a cash sale the buyer takes the house as it stands, and any unpaid tax gets cleared at closing.

There is no lender in the middle, so there is no appraisal and no repair list to haggle over. Start by telling us about the house. We look at it as it is and, if it fits, send an offer in writing. If you accept, you pick the closing date and a title company sets it up.

At closing the title company confirms the deed, pays off the mortgage or tax balance out of your proceeds and records the transfer. You can leave the paint and minor fixes alone.

We buy homes that need repairs, homes that came through an inheritance and homes with tenants in them. Weigh any offer against the cost of listing: repairs, months of carrying costs and the chance a financed buyer walks away.

sections.h2: Timeline from first call to closing
sections.html:
Most of the waiting in a traditional sale comes from the buyer's side: loan approval, the lender's appraisal and a round of repair requests after the inspection. A cash purchase removes those steps. The pace then depends on the title search, any payoff letters and the date you choose.

If a mortgage is still open, ask the lender for a payoff figure early. If an estate is involved, the person with authority to sell should be ready to sign. Sorting these two items first is what keeps a closing date from slipping.

A short folder saves days. Include your latest tax bill, a payoff statement if a mortgage remains, permit records for any past additions and, when you inherited the property, the papers that show who may sign for the estate.

One call to the Town confirming that the parcel is inside the limits, and whether any code case is open, removes two common surprises from closing week.

faqs.q: What county is Lexington, SC in?
faqs.a: Lexington is the county seat of Lexington County. The county handles tax bills and deed recording, while the town handles zoning, permits and code enforcement inside its limits.

faqs.q: When are Lexington County property taxes due?
faqs.a: Pay between September 30 and January 15 to avoid penalties. Miss that window and the bill grows by 3% first, then 7% from February 1, then 5% from March 16.

faqs.q: Can I pay Lexington County property taxes in installments?
faqs.a: Yes, if you apply before January 15 and your taxes are not escrowed. Five advance payments of 16.67% of last year's tax fall due between February 15 and October 15, and you settle the balance on January 15.

faqs.q: What does it take to record a deed in Lexington County?
faqs.a: Bring the deed and an affidavit for the transfer, and pay the state fee of $1.85 per $500 of value. The filing office is the Register of Deeds, 212 S. Lake Dr., Suite 301.

faqs.q: Does Lake Murray change how I sell my Lexington house?
faqs.a: It can. Lake-adjacent parcels may involve shoreline, dock and flood questions that other houses do not, so ask your title company about your parcel.
